810 Vermont Ave NW 
Washington, DC 20420 
 
RE: Reproductive Health Services, RIN 2900-AS31, 38 CFR Part 17 
The Jacobs Institute of Women’s Health urges the Veterans Administration (VA) to withdraw its 
proposed “Reproductive Health Services” rule (RIN 2900-AS31), which would reinstate exclusions on 
abortions and abortion counseling from its medical benefits package. 
The mission of Jacobs Institute of Women's Health is to identify and study aspects of healthcare and 
public health, including legal and policy issues, that affect women’s health at different life stages; to 
foster awareness of and facilitate dialogue around issues that affect women’s health; and to promote 
interdisciplinary research, coordination, and information dissemination, including publishing the peer-
reviewed journal Women's Health Issues. We represent an interdisciplinary group of affiliated faculty 
members who are experts in research, health policy, and medical care related to women’s health. 
Abortion is healthcare, and VA should offer all pregnant veterans access to abortion care. The recent 
change VA now seeks to undo took small but essential steps toward doing so by 1) removing the 
exclusion on abortion counseling and 2) allowing abortions when the pregnancy endangers the life or 
health of the pregnant veteran and when the pregnancy is the result of rape or incest (as self-reported 
by the veteran).1 
Compared to the general population, veterans have higher rates of gestational diabetes and 
hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, which make pregnancy more risky.2 Military sexual trauma (MST) 
is common among women veterans — in a recent survey, 69% of post-9/11 women veterans who used 
VA reproductive healthcare reported a history of MST3 — and often leads to post-traumatic stress 
 
1 Veterans Aﬀairs Department. (2022). Reproduc9ve Health Services. Federal Register, RIN 2900-AR57. 
hFps://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2022/09/09/2022-19239/reproduc9ve-health-services 
2 Katon J, MaFocks K, Zephyrin L, Reiber G, Yano EM, Callegari L, Schwarz EB, Goulet J, Shaw J, Brandt C, & Haskell S. 
(2014). Gesta9onal Diabetes and Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy Among Women Veterans Deployed in 
Service of Opera9ons in Afghanistan and Iraq. Journal of Women’s Health, 23(10):792-800. 
3 Monteith L, KiFel JA, Schneider AL, Miller CN, Holliday R, Katon JG, Brenner LA, & Hoﬀmire CA. (2024). Military 
Sexual Trauma Among Women Veterans Using Veterans Health Administra9on Reproduc9ve Health Care: Screening 
Challenges and Associa9ons with Post-Military Suicidal Idea9on and Suicide AFempts. Journal of Interpersonal 
Violence, 38(11-12):7578-7601. 

disorder (PTSD).4 Veterans experiencing PTSD while pregnant face a 35% higher risk of preterm birth5 
and 30% higher risk of preeclampsia.6 
Servicewomen face the risk of rape not only during military service but also from their partners. Intimate 
partner violence is highly prevalent among veterans; 46% of women veterans in a 2020 national survey 
reported having experienced it.7  
Dangerous heath conditions during pregnancy and rape are both common among women veterans, and 
it is unsurprising that veterans facing either or both would seek abortions. The 2022 interim final rule 
allowing for pregnancy options counseling and abortion coverage in limited circumstances was therefore 
responsive to a need for high-quality care among veterans. VA should retain the 2022 changes to its 
medical benefits package, or it should change the regulation to make abortion available to all veterans. 
Re-imposing restrictions on care would mark a step backwards in the quality of care for veterans, who 
deserve care that meets the highest standards and their needs. 
For these reasons, the Jacobs Institute of Women’s Health opposes the rule change. Thank you for the 
opportunity to comment.

1119.

Disorder and Antepartum Complica9ons: A Novel Risk Factor for Gesta9onal Diabetes and Preeclampsia. Paediatric 
Perinatal Epidemiology, 31(3):185-194.

Violence and In9mate Partner Violence Among US Military Veterans: Findings from Surveys with Two Na9onal 
Samples. Journal of General Internal Medicine, 39(3):418-427.
